name: Anatomical Models and 3D Printing
title: Anatomical Models and 3D Printing
answer: Anatomical models and 3D printing in radiology covers patient-specific physical and digital replicas built from CT, MRI, ultrasound, and other volumetric imaging. The models can show bones, vessels, tumors, airways, and congenital defects for surgical planning, trainee education, device fitting, and communication with patients and families. The field sits inside diagnostic imaging because the source data and the segmentation work begin with radiology studies. AI segmentation models are part of the 1000 medical AI models this site tracks, and they increasingly feed these workflows.

sections.body: Anatomical models and 3D printing in radiology covers patient-specific physical and digital replicas built from CT, MRI, ultrasound, and other volumetric imaging. The models can show bones, vessels, tumors, airways, and congenital defects for surgical planning, trainee education, device fitting, and communication with patients and families. The field sits inside diagnostic imaging because the source data and the segmentation work begin with radiology studies. AI segmentation models are part of the 1000 medical AI models this site tracks, and they increasingly feed these workflows.
sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: The pipeline runs on a radiology workstation or server that can handle DICOM image series, segmentation software, and mesh editing tools. Output goes to a 3D printer, usually material extrusion or resin, or to a viewing platform for digital models. Common materials include photopolymer resins, thermoplastics, and sometimes flexible or biocompatible resins for specific uses. Storage, compute, and network capacity matter because volumetric studies are large and print files can be large as well.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: The work starts with image acquisition and quality checks, then segmentation of the anatomy of interest, either manual, semi-automatic, or AI-assisted. The segmented mask is converted into a surface mesh, often as an STL file, then repaired, smoothed, and hollowed or thickened as needed for printing. A radiologist or surgeon reviews the model against the source images before it is used in planning or education. Printing parameters, material choice, and post-processing are recorded so the model can be reproduced or compared. Validation may include dimensional checks, fit tests, and review by the clinical team.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: Rights and risk center on patient privacy, consent for creating and using a model, and clear provenance from the source study to the final print. A printed model is a derived dataset, so it inherits the same protections as the underlying images and must be handled under the same institutional rules. Accuracy matters because an error in segmentation or printing can mislead a surgical plan, so quality control and traceability are part of the record. Regulatory status varies by jurisdiction and by intended use, with models for diagnosis or treatment planning facing more scrutiny than models for education. Liability questions can arise if a model is defective or misused, and the wider rules for medical AI and software as a medical device often shape how these workflows are documented.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: The direction of travel is toward faster, more automated segmentation and mesh preparation, with AI models reducing manual steps. Point-of-care printing in hospitals and clinics is expanding, along with materials that better mimic tissue and bone. Digital twins, augmented reality, and mixed reality are being paired with printed models for planning and education. Regulatory pathways and quality standards are still maturing, so reproducibility and documentation will likely remain central. The field will continue to sit between radiology, surgery, engineering, and medical illustration, with the source imaging and the clinical question always setting the limits.
